    Our story
    Nature, people and water.
    Aquatic World starts from a simple idea: the beauty of a living landscape can travel, if it is chosen and handled with care. The story page sets out the perspective behind the brand.
    Bringing the beauty of nature a little further.
    Read our story 
  



  
    
      Quality
      Care in every step, stated plainly.
      Four proposed principles that guide selection and handling. They describe an approach, not a certification.
      See the full approach 
    
    
      Select with questionsEvery choice starts from the display it is meant for.
      Observe before offeringCondition and behaviour are watched, not assumed.
      Handle with intentPacking is planned for the journey, not for appearance.
      Follow up honestlyAsk how things settled and say what is unknown.

      Collections
      Three collection families
    
    
      A good aquatic display is a composition: something that moves, a landscape that grows and a structure that holds it together. Start with the family you need, or read how they work together below.
      01Ornamental Fish02Aquatic Plants03Driftwood
    
  



  
    
    
    
      01 Collection
      Ornamental Fish
      Fish bring movement and colour to a composition. This family is presented as studies of form and finnage, with selection framed as questions to discuss rather than a stock list.
      Colour and finnageForm and movementCommunity fit
      Explore ornamental fish 
    
  
    
    
    
      02 Collection
      Aquatic Plants
      Plants build depth and atmosphere. This family is organised around how foliage shapes a scape — layer, leaf form, colour and texture — not around a catalogue of species.
      Layer and depthLeaf form and textureColour contrast
      Explore aquatic plants 
    
  
    
    
    
      03 Collection
      Driftwood
      Driftwood is the structure of a scape. Each piece is discussed by its lines, branching and mass, and by how its surface reads under water and light.
      Line and branchingMass and scaleSurface and tone
      Explore driftwood

        Aquatic Plants

        Prepare a fish enquiry

      StudiesColour and form, side by side.

        Study 01Single-colour, long-finned formDeep red throughout; the spread of the fins carries most of the visual weight.

      Selection considerations
      What shapes a fish selection
      Framed as questions for a conversation. Care requirements vary by fish and should be confirmed for each case.
    
    
      i.Colour and finnageIs colour meant to lead the display or accent it? Long fins read beautifully in calm water but change how a fish fits with others.
      ii.Form and movementTall, slow-moving forms suit open water; small, quick fish bring life to planted edges. Movement is part of the composition.
      iii.Community fitWhich inhabitants are already there or planned? Temperament and pace matter as much as appearance.
      iv.Display contextViewing distance, lighting and background colour all change how a fish is seen. A dark planted scape and a bright open tank ask for different choices.

      A short, specific brief makes the first conversation useful. The contact page will start with ornamental fish selected.

      Composition
      How plants shape an aquascape
      Most planted displays read in three layers. Thinking in layers makes it easier to describe what a scape needs.
      
        3BackgroundTall, upright growth that gives height and hides the back of the display.
        2MidgroundBushier forms that bridge the layers and soften hardscape edges.
        1ForegroundLow, fine growth that keeps the front open and creates a sense of depth.
      
    
    
      
        Diagram: a display seen from the front, with a tall background layer, a medium midground layer and a low foreground layer.
        
        
        
        
        
          3
          2
          1
        
      
      Front view, simplified. Proportions are illustrative.
    
  



  
    
      
      Illustrative study: red and bronze foliage against green.
    
    
      Visual characteristics
      What to look at in a plant
      
        Leaf formBroad leaves read as calm surfaces; fine leaves and stems read as texture and movement.
        ColourMost scapes are built on greens. A single group of red or bronze foliage becomes a focal point.
        TextureMixing coarse and fine textures helps each layer stay distinct from a distance.
        Growth habitUpright, spreading or carpeting growth decides where a plant belongs in the layers.
      
    
  



  
    
      Enquiry context
      Questions to plan a plant enquiry around
      A short, specific brief makes the first conversation useful. The contact page will start with aquatic plants selected.
      Prepare a plant enquiry

      Structure
      Structure sets the composition
      
        Lines lead the eyeThe main direction of a piece decides how a viewer moves through the display.
        Mass sets the scaleA heavy base grounds the scene; fine branches make a display feel larger than it is.
        Space lets it breatheLeaving open water beside the structure gives fish room to be seen.
      
    
  



  
    
      Material
      Reading the material
      Visual notes for choosing between pieces. Preparation and suitability depend on the individual piece and display, and should be confirmed case by case.
    
    
      SilhouetteSeen from the main viewing side, does the outline have one clear direction or several competing ones?
      BranchingDense, fine branching creates detail and shelter; few heavy limbs create a bolder, calmer shape.
      SurfaceDeep grooves and worn edges catch light differently from smooth wood, and plants attach to them differently.
      ToneWarm brown tones contrast with green planting; darker wood recedes into a dark background.
    
  



  
    
      Enquiry context
      Planning a hardscape enquiry
      A short, specific brief makes the first conversation useful. The contact page will start with driftwood selected.

    Our story
    Bringing the beauty of nature a little further.
    A proposed perspective for the Aquatic World brand: why living water matters, who it is for, and how it should be handled.
  



  
  Illustrative waterfront scene. It does not depict company premises or a confirmed location.



  
    
      I
      Nature
      A planted aquarium is a small landscape that keeps changing. Light moves through leaves, wood softens with time and fish settle into the spaces left for them. The brand begins from respect for that living quality — the idea that a display is grown and looked after, not simply assembled.
    
    
      II
      People
      The people behind a beautiful display are rarely seen: the retailer who advises a first-time keeper, the aquascaper who spends weeks on a single layout, the enthusiast who rebuilds a tank until it feels right. Aquatic World is imagined as a partner to them — useful in conversation, careful in what it promises.
    
    Good aquatic things travel far — when they are chosen with care.
    
      III
      Water
      Water connects every part of the work, from the place a plant grows to the display where it finally sits. Moving living things through water asks for patience and honesty about what can and cannot be known in advance. That is where quality starts.
    
  



  
  Still water. Slow decisions.



  
    
      Proposed values
      What the brand would stand for
      Draft values for discussion; they would need to be confirmed by a real organisation before public use.
    
    
      Composition over collectionHelp people build displays that work as a whole, not lists of items.
      Care that can be explainedEvery handling decision should have a reason someone can ask about.
      Honesty about the unknownSay clearly what is illustrative, uncertain or still to be confirmed.

      Quality
      A thoughtful selection process, explained.
    
    
      Quality in living goods is mostly about decisions made before anything moves. This page sets out what a careful process should consider and the questions worth asking.
      Proposed principles. Aquatic World is an illustrative concept. Nothing on this page is a certification, guarantee or audited standard.
    
  



  
    
      The processFive considerations, in order
      Each step pairs a principle with a question a buyer can reasonably ask.
    
    
      
        01
        Sourcing
        Know where each item comes from and keep a record that can be shared.
        AskWhere does this come from, and how is that recorded?
      
        02
        Observation
        Allow time to watch condition and behaviour before anything is offered.
        AskHow long is something observed before it is offered?
      
        03
        Preparation
        Plan holding and acclimation around the receiving display, not a generic routine.
        AskWhat do you need to know about my setup?
      
        04
        Handling & packing
        Pack for the journey and the conditions, and keep handling to a minimum.
        AskHow is packing adapted to distance and timing?
      
        05
        Follow-up
        Ask how things settled and record what should change next time.
        AskWhat happens if something does not settle well?
      
    
  



  
    
      
      Illustrative study image.
    
    
      Practical questions
      Questions worth asking any supplier
      
        What information comes with each item?
        How are condition and behaviour checked?
        How is packing chosen for distance and timing?
        What should be ready before arrival?
        Who can I talk to if something looks wrong?
        What cannot be known in advance?
      
    
  



  
    
      Expectations
      Reasonable expectations, on both sides
    
    
      What a supplier can describeHow items are selected, observed, packed and followed up — and what records exist.
      What depends on the receiverA prepared display, a plan for arrival and honest information about the setup.
      What no one can promiseLiving things vary. Clear communication matters more than guarantees.
    
  



  
    Have specific requirements?
    Note them in an enquiry brief so they can be discussed first.
    Discuss requirements
